paragraphs: In the character of these states, whether republics or despotisms, lies, not the only, but the chief reason for the early development of the Italian. To this it is due that he was the first-born among the sons of modern Europe.

In the Middle Ages both sides of human consciousness—that which was turned within as that which was turned without—lay dreaming or half-awake beneath a common veil. The veil was woven of faith, illusion, and childish prepossession, through which the world and history were seen clad in strange hues. Man was conscious of himself only as member of a race, people, party, family, or corporation—only through some general category. In Italy this veil first melted into air; an objective treatment and consideration of the state and of all the things of this world became possible. The subjective side at the same time asserted itself with corresponding emphasis; man became a spiritual individual, and recognised himself as such. … It will not be difficult to show that this result was owing above all to the political circumstances of Italy.

… at the close of the thirteenth century Italy began to swarm with individuality; the charm laid upon human personality was dissolved; and a thousand figures meet us each in its own special shape and dress. … Despotism, as we have already seen, fostered in the highest degree the individuality not only of the tyrant or Condottiere himself, but also of the men whom he protected or used as his tools—the secretary, minister, poet, and companion.

paragraphs: My intention is to demonstrate briefly and clearly that the Dutch—that is to say, the subjects of the United Netherlands—have the right to sail to the East Indies, as they are now doing, and to engage in trade with the people there. X3.caption: Two men stand on either side of a two-level table in front of a green curtain. The man on the left wears rich clothes trimmed with fur and a gold chain. The man on the right wears a long dark robe. On the top level, which is covered with a patterned carpet, are a globe of the heavens and several instruments for measuring the sun and stars, such as sundials and a quadrant. X3.description: A life-size double portrait painted in oil. Against a heavy green damask curtain, two young men stand facing the viewer. On the left, Jean de Dinteville wears a black velvet coat lined with white fur over a pink satin shirt, a black cap, and a gold chain with a medallion, and he holds a dagger in a gold sheath. On the right, Georges de Selve wears a long dark brown robe lined with fur and a square black cap, and rests his arm on the table. Between them stands a wooden table with two shelves. The upper shelf is covered by a red and blue patterned carpet from the Middle East and holds a celestial globe, a cylinder-shaped sundial, a brass quadrant, a many-sided sundial, and another instrument for measuring the positions of the stars. The lower shelf holds a terrestrial globe, a book on arithmetic for merchants with a ruler inside it, a lute with a broken string, a case of flutes, a pair of dividers, and an open hymnbook showing words and music. Across the patterned stone floor in the foreground lies a long, pale, slanted shape that looks like a smear when seen from the front but becomes a human skull when seen from a sharp angle at the side. In the top left corner, half hidden by the curtain, is a small silver crucifix.

X4.text: Rogers estimated the grain a family needed for a year (three quarters of wheat, three of malt, and two of oatmeal; a quarter is eight bushels). For each year, he compared the price of that grain with daily wages: wages actually paid in 1495, and wages set by local officials in Rutland in 1564 and in the East Riding of Yorkshire in 1593. These are estimates for selected places, not averages for all of England. Wheat prices were unusually high in 1564.

paragraphs: … They say the city of Rome is theirs, theirs the kingdom of Sicily and of Naples, the whole of Italy, the Gauls, the Spains, the Germans, the Britons, indeed the whole West; for all these are contained in the instrument of the Donation* itself. So all these are yours, supreme pontiff? And it is your purpose to recover them all? To despoil all kings and princes of the West of their cities or compel them to pay you a yearly tribute, is that your plan?

I, on the contrary, think it fairer to let the princes despoil you of all the empire you hold. For, as I shall show, that Donation whence the supreme pontiffs will have their right derived was unknown equally to Sylvester and to Constantine. …

"In this privilege, among other things, is this: We—together with all our satraps and the whole Senate and the nobles also, and all the people subject to the government of the Roman church—considered it advisable that, as the blessed Peter is seen to have been constituted vicar of God on the earth, so the pontiffs who are the representatives of that same chief of the apostles, should obtain from us and our Empire the power of a supremacy greater than the clemency of our earthly imperial serenity is seen to have conceded to it."

O thou scoundrel, thou villain! … What! How do you want to have satraps come in here? Numskull, blockhead! Do the Caesars speak thus; are Roman decrees usually drafted thus? Whoever heard of satraps being mentioned in the councils of the Romans? I do not remember ever to have read of any Roman satrap being mentioned, or even of a satrap in any of the Roman provinces.

paragraphs: … the authority of the Star-chamber,* which before subsisted by the ancient common laws of the realm, was confirmed in certain cases by act of parliament. … But that which was principally aimed at by this act was force, and the two chief supports of force, combination of multitudes, and maintenance or headship of great persons.

… There remaineth to this day a report that the king was on a time entertained by the earl of Oxford, that was his principal servant both for war and peace, nobly and sumptuously, at his castle at Henningham: and at the king's going away, the earl's servants stood, in a seemly manner, in their livery coats, with cognizances, ranged on both sides, and made the king a lane. The king called the earl to him, and said, "My lord, I have heard much of your hospitality, but I see it is greater than the speech: these handsome gentlemen and yeomen, which I see on both sides of me, are sure your menial servants." The earl smiled, and said, "It may please your grace, that were not for mine own ease: they are most of them my retainers, that are come to do me service at such a time as this, and chiefly to see your grace." The king started a little, and said, "By my faith, my lord, I thank you for my good cheer, but I may not endure to have my laws broken in my sight; my attorney must speak with you." And it is part of the report, that the earl compounded for no less than fifteen thousand marks.
… As for riot and retainers, there passed scarce any parliament in this time without a law against them: the king ever having an eye to might and multitude.

paragraphs: Your Reverence writes me that you would like to know whether the negroes who are sent to your parts have been legally captured. To this I reply that I think your Reverence should have no scruples on this point, because this is a matter which has been questioned by the Board of Conscience in Lisbon, and all its members are learned and conscientious men. Nor did the bishops who were in São Thomé, Cape Verde, and here in Loando—all learned and virtuous men—find fault with it. We have been here ourselves for forty years and there have been [among us] very learned Fathers; in the Province of Brazil as well, where there have always been Fathers of our order eminent in letters, never did they consider this trade as illicit. Therefore we and the fathers of Brazil buy these slaves for our service without any scruple. …

… I declare, moreover, that in the fairs where these negroes are bought there are always a few who have been captured illegally because they were stolen or because the rulers of the land order them to be sold for offenses so slight that they do not deserve captivity, but these are few in number and to seek among ten or twelve thousand who leave this port every year for a few who have been illegally captured is an impossibility, however careful investigation may be made. And to lose so many souls as sail from here—out of whom many are saved—because some, impossible to recognize, have been captured illegally does not seem to be doing much service to God, for these are few and those who find salvation are many and legally captured.

paragraphs: Your Cicero has been in my possession four years and more. There is a good reason, though, for so long a delay; namely, the great scarcity of copyists who understand such work. It is a state of affairs that has resulted in an incredible loss to scholarship. Books that by their nature are a little hard to understand are no longer multiplied, and have ceased to be generally intelligible, and so have sunk into utter neglect, and in the end have perished. This age of ours consequently has let fall, bit by bit, some of the richest and sweetest fruits that the tree of knowledge has yielded; has thrown away the results of the vigils and labours of the most illustrious men of genius, things of more value, I am almost tempted to say, than anything else in the whole world. …

But I must return to your Cicero. I could not do without it, and the incompetence of the copyists would not let me possess it. What was left for me but to rely upon my own resources, and press these weary fingers and this worn and ragged pen into the service? … Not a single word did I read except as I wrote. … So the pen held back the eye, and the eye drove on the pen, and I covered page after page, delighting in my task, and committing many and many a passage to memory as I wrote.
… I said to myself, "So Cicero copied orations that another wrote, and you are not ready to copy his? What ardour! what scholarly devotion! what reverence for a man of godlike genius!"

paragraphs: Nothing makes a prince so well thought of as to undertake great enterprises and give striking proofs of his capacity.

Among the princes of our time Ferdinand of Aragon, the present king of Spain, may almost be accounted a new prince, since from one of the weakest he has become, for fame and glory, the foremost king in Christendom. And if you consider his achievements, you will find them all great, and some extraordinary.

In the beginning of his reign he made war on Granada, which enterprise was the foundation of his power. At first he carried on the war leisurely, without fear of interruption, and kept the attention and thoughts of the barons of Castile so completely occupied with it that they had no time to think of changes at home. Meanwhile he insensibly acquired reputation among them and authority over them. With the money of the Church and of his subjects he was able to maintain his armies, and during the prolonged contest to lay the foundations of that military discipline which afterwards made him so famous.

Moreover, to enable him to engage in still greater undertakings, always covering himself with the cloak of religion, he had recourse to what may be called "pious cruelty," in driving out and clearing his kingdom of the Moors;* than which exploit none could be more wonderful or uncommon. Using the same pretext, he made war on Africa, invaded Italy, and finally attacked France …

paragraphs: B. There you might have seen a miserable condition of affairs. The sailors, singing "Salve, regina," implored the Virgin mother, calling her star of the sea, queen of heaven, ruler of the world, harbor of safety, and flattering her with many other titles, which the holy scriptures nowhere attribute to her. …

B. Some were sufficiently occupied with sea-sickness; but most of them offered vows. Among them was a certain Englishman, who promised mountains of gold to our Lady of Walsingham, if only he might touch land alive. Some promised many things to the wood of the cross, which was in such a place; others again to the same in another place. …
A. … What were you doing all this time? Did you offer vows to none of the saints?
B. Not one.
A. Why not?

B. Because I do not drive bargains with the saints. For what is it other than a contract according to form? "I will give this, if you will do that; I will give you a wax candle, if I swim out of this; I will go to Rome, if you will save me." …
A. What did you do, then?
B. I went immediately to the Father himself, saying: "Our Father who art in heaven." None of the saints hears sooner than He, nor gives more willingly what is asked.

paragraphs: 'The increase of pasture,' said I, 'by which your sheep, which are naturally mild, and easily kept in order, may be said now to devour men, and unpeople, not only villages, but towns; for wherever it is found that the sheep of any soil yield a softer and richer wool than ordinary, there the nobility and gentry, and even those holy men the abbots, not contented with the old rents which their farms yielded, nor thinking it enough that they, living at their ease, do no good to the public, resolve to do it hurt instead of good. They stop the course of agriculture, destroying houses and towns, reserving only the churches, and enclose grounds that they may lodge their sheep in them. …

… the owners as well as tenants are turned out of their possessions, by tricks, or by main force, or being wearied out with ill-usage, they are forced to sell them. By which means those miserable people, both men and women, married and unmarried, old and young, with their poor but numerous families (since country business requires many hands), are all forced to change their seats, not knowing whither to go … When that little money is at an end, for it will be soon spent, what is left for them to do, but either to steal and so to be hanged (God knows how justly), or to go about and beg? And if they do this, they are put in prison as idle vagabonds; while they would willingly work, but can find none that will hire them; for there is no more occasion for country labor, to which they have been bred, when there is no arable ground left. paragraphs: … I find that there is nothing barbarous and savage in this nation, by anything that I can gather, excepting, that every one gives the title of barbarism to everything that is not in use in his own country. As, indeed, we have no other level of truth and reason, than the example and idea of the opinions and customs of the place wherein we live: there is always the perfect religion, there the perfect government, there the most exact and accomplished usage of all things. …

… I am not sorry that we should here take notice of the barbarous horror of so cruel an action,* but that, seeing so clearly into their faults, we should be so blind to our own. I conceive there is more barbarity in eating a man alive, than when he is dead; in tearing a body limb from limb by racks and torments, that is yet in perfect sense; in roasting it by degrees; in causing it to be bitten and worried by dogs and swine (as we have not only read, but lately seen, not amongst inveterate and mortal enemies, but among neighbours and fellow-citizens, and, which is worse, under colour of piety and religion), than to roast and eat him after he is dead.

… The first bullocks I saw at the plough were in the valley of Cuzco in the year 1550, one year more or less … A whole army of Indians took me to see them, who came from all parts, astonished at a sight so wonderful and novel for them and for me. They said that the Spaniards were too idle to work, and that they forced those great animals to do their work for them. …

… There were no sugar canes; but at present, owing to the diligence of the Spaniards, and the great fertility of the land, there is such abundance of all these things that, while at first they were valued so highly, they are now despised and held very cheap. … Many sugar estates have since been established in Peru.

paragraphs: In order that the subjects of His Illustrious Highness, the most honorable and magnanimous Duke of Urbino … may have all the rules that a good merchant needs, I decided to compile, in addition to the subjects already treated in this work, a special treatise which is much needed. … For, as we know, there are three things needed by any one who wishes to carry on business carefully. The most important of these is cash or any equivalent … Without this, business can hardly be carried on.

It has happened that many without capital of their own but whose credit was good, carried on big transactions and by means of their credit, which they faithfully kept, became very wealthy. We became acquainted with many of these throughout Italy. In the great republics nothing was considered superior to the word of the good merchant, and oaths were taken on the word of a good merchant. On this confidence rested the faith they had in the trustworthiness of an upright merchant. And this is not strange, because, according to the Christian religion, we are saved by faith, and without it it is impossible to please God.

The second thing necessary in business is to be a good bookkeeper and ready mathematician. … The third and last thing is to arrange all the transactions in such a systematic way that one may understand each one of them at a glance, i. e., by the debit … and credit … method. This is very essential to merchants, because, without making the entries systematically it would be impossible to conduct their business, for they would have no rest and their minds would always be troubled. … This treatise will adopt the system used in Venice, which is certainly to be recommended above all the others …

practice.stem: Petrarch's main concern in the first paragraph is that

options.A: ancient works were being lost because few people could copy them well
options.B: the Church had forbidden scholars to read pagan Roman writers
options.C: printers were filling the market with careless copies of old books
options.D: Latin had been replaced by Italian as the main language taught in the schools of Florence

practice.explanation: Petrarch says hard books "are no longer multiplied." In the end, he says, they "have perished." Without good copyists, the works of ancient writers were being lost.

whyNot.B: There was no such ban. Monks had copied Roman writers like Cicero for centuries.
whyNot.C: Printing with movable type did not begin in Europe until the 1450s, about a hundred years after this letter. Petrarch's problem was a shortage of skilled people who copied by hand.
whyNot.D: Petrarch does not mention schools. Latin stayed the language of learning in European schools for centuries.

practice.hint: Reread the sentences about copyists and about books that "have perished." What is Petrarch afraid of?

practice.stem: Petrarch's attitude toward Cicero best illustrates which of the following?

options.A: the scholastic use of Aristotle to explain Christian beliefs
options.B: the Christian humanist call to translate the Bible into everyday languages
options.C: the humanist revival of interest in ancient Roman writers
options.D: the Renaissance artist's study of the human body

practice.explanation: Petrarch is often called the father of humanism. He searched for old Roman books and copied them by hand. He even calls Cicero a man of "godlike genius." This love of classical texts was at the heart of the Italian Renaissance.

whyNot.A: Scholastics such as Thomas Aquinas used Aristotle's logic to explain Christian teaching. Petrarch admires Cicero's own writing and his "godlike genius."
whyNot.B: Christian humanists such as Erasmus later wanted the Bible studied in its original languages and read in everyday languages. Petrarch is copying a work by a pagan Roman, not the Bible.
whyNot.D: Artists such as Leonardo studied anatomy. Petrarch's letter is about copying a book, not about art.

practice.hint: What kind of writer is Cicero, and how does Petrarch feel about him?

practice.stem: The problem Petrarch describes in the first paragraph was most directly reduced by which later development?

options.A: The fall of Constantinople to the Ottoman Turks
options.B: The printing press
options.C: The founding of monastery writing rooms
options.D: The Catholic Church's Index of Forbidden Books

practice.explanation: Printing with movable type spread from Mainz, in Germany, after the 1450s. A printer could make hundreds of copies of a book like Cicero's, so rare works were far less likely to be lost.

whyNot.A: When Constantinople fell in 1453, Greek scholars and books came to Italy. That added texts, but it did not solve the shortage of people who could copy them.
whyNot.C: Monasteries had used writing rooms to copy books by hand since the early Middle Ages, long before Petrarch. Hand copying was the slow method he complained about.
whyNot.D: The Index, first issued in 1559, banned certain books. It limited reading instead of making more copies.

practice.hint: Think about what happened about a hundred years after this letter that changed how books were made.

practice.stem: Federico's spending on his library was most likely intended to

options.A: provide cheap books for the ordinary people of Urbino
options.B: challenge the pope's authority over Christian teaching
options.C: train the merchants of Urbino in new methods of trade
options.D: show off his learning and raise his prestige as a ruler

practice.explanation: Renaissance rulers spent huge sums on art, buildings, and books. Federico had grown rich by fighting wars for other states. A great library showed that he was also a man of learning. That raised his prestige.

whyNot.A: The library cost "more than 30,000 ducats," and its books were written by hand on kid-skin. They were treasures for a court, not cheap books for ordinary people.
whyNot.B: The library held the Bible and Christian writers. Federico was a Catholic ruler, and the pope made him Duke of Urbino in 1474.
whyNot.C: The passage lists Greek, Hebrew, and religious works, not business books.

practice.hint: Look at the cost of the library and how its books were made. Whom would such a library impress?

practice.stem: Federico's collection of Greek and Hebrew books best reflects which humanist goal?

options.A: replacing Latin with Italian as the language of learning
options.B: reading ancient texts in their original languages
options.C: rejecting Christian writings in favor of pagan ones
options.D: keeping ancient learning away from the clergy

practice.explanation: Humanists wanted to read Plato, Homer, and the Bible in Greek and Hebrew. They did not want to rely only on Latin translations. Reading texts in the first language was part of a new, careful way of study.

whyNot.A: The library is filled with Greek, Hebrew, and Latin works. Humanists studied the classical languages more, not less.
whyNot.C: The library includes the Bible and its commentators alongside Plato and Homer. Humanists combined pagan and Christian learning.
whyNot.D: Popes and churchmen were among the greatest collectors of ancient books. Pope Nicholas V founded what became the Vatican Library.

practice.hint: Why would a collector want the works of Aristotle "in Greek" and the Bible in Hebrew?

practice.stem: Vespasiano's remark that none of the books in the library was printed best supports which conclusion?

options.A: Some rich collectors at first valued handwritten books more.
options.B: Printing had not yet reached Italy when Federico built his library.
options.C: The Church had forbidden Italian rulers to own printed books.
options.D: Printed books cost more than books written on kid-skin.

practice.explanation: Federico wanted every book "written with the pen." He did not want the library to be "disgraced" by printing. To some rich collectors, a hand-painted book was a work of art. A printed book seemed cheap and common.

whyNot.B: German printers set up presses in Italy in 1465, and Venice became a printing center in the 1470s. Federico could have bought printed books, but he chose not to.
whyNot.C: There was no such ban. Popes and cardinals bought and supported printed books too.
whyNot.D: Printed books were usually much cheaper, since many copies could be made at once. That is one reason a proud collector looked down on them.

practice.hint: Check each choice against what you know about when printing reached Italy and what printed books cost.

practice.stem: Leonardo most likely wrote this letter in order to

options.A: warn Milan's ruler that warfare threatened artists and scholars
options.B: ask Milan's ruler to protect the privileges of painters' guilds
options.C: win a position in the service of Milan's ruler
options.D: persuade Milan's ruler to buy weapons from other Italian states

practice.explanation: Renaissance artists needed rich patrons. Leonardo lists all the things he can do, especially for war. He wants the ruler of Milan to hire him. Leonardo did move to Milan in the early 1480s and worked for Ludovico for years.

whyNot.A: Leonardo offers to build bridges, mortars, and big guns for war. He does not warn the ruler against war.
whyNot.B: Leonardo promotes his own skills. He does not ask for anything on behalf of a guild.
whyNot.D: Leonardo offers weapons he can make himself: "I will make big guns, mortars and light ordnance."

practice.hint: What does Leonardo offer, and to whom?

practice.stem: The skills Leonardo stresses most are best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.A: Frequent wars among the Italian states
options.B: The Spanish war to conquer Granada
options.C: Medici patronage of artists in Florence
options.D: Portugal's voyages along the coast of Africa

practice.explanation: Italy was split into rival states, such as Milan, Venice, Florence, Naples, and the Papal States. They often fought one another. So rulers wanted engineers who could build bridges, guns, and siege machines.

whyNot.B: Spain's war on Granada began in 1482, but Leonardo is writing to the ruler of Milan. Milan took no part in that war.
whyNot.C: Lorenzo de' Medici did support artists in Florence. But Leonardo is writing to the ruler of Milan, and most of the skills he lists are for war, not art.
whyNot.D: Portuguese sailors were exploring the coast of Africa in the 1480s. But Leonardo offers bridges, mortars, and big guns to use against an enemy, not ships for voyages of discovery.

practice.hint: Most of Leonardo's list is weapons and war machines. Why would the ruler of Milan want them?

practice.stem: The kind of military technology Leonardo describes later helped European states expand overseas mainly by

options.A: giving armed ships and forts the power to control ports and sea routes
options.B: letting small European armies conquer the Ming and Mughal empires in the 1500s
options.C: allowing the Spanish to defeat the Aztec and Inca empires without Native allies
options.D: breaking the Ottoman Empire's control of the eastern Mediterranean Sea

practice.explanation: Cannons let Europeans attack or defend ships and coastal forts. In the early 1500s, Portugal used this firepower to seize ports such as Goa and Malacca and to control key sea routes in the Indian Ocean.

whyNot.B: European guns gave them power at sea and along coasts, but the great land empires of Asia, such as Ming China and Mughal India, stayed strong. Europeans held only small trading posts there, such as Goa and Macau.
whyNot.C: Guns and horses helped the Spanish, but they also depended on thousands of Native allies, such as the Tlaxcalans who fought beside Cortés, and on diseases that killed many Native people.
whyNot.D: The Ottomans kept their power in the eastern Mediterranean even after their defeat at Lepanto in 1571. Portugal and Spain expanded by sailing around Africa and across the Atlantic instead.

practice.hint: Leonardo's inventions are for fighting. Think about how Portugal won trading ports in Asia.

practice.stem: Machiavelli's main point about Ferdinand is that he

options.A: lost power because he depended on money from the Church
options.B: ruled weakly because the barons of Castile controlled him
options.C: grew powerful through bold wars and the clever use of religion
options.D: succeeded mainly by keeping peace with his neighbors

practice.explanation: Machiavelli says Ferdinand went from a weak king to "the foremost king in Christendom." He started great wars and kept the nobles busy. He also hid his aims under "the cloak of religion."

whyNot.A: Machiavelli says Ferdinand used "the money of the Church and of his subjects" to keep his armies. That money helped him gain power.
whyNot.B: Machiavelli says the war kept the barons busy. Meanwhile Ferdinand gained "authority over them."
whyNot.D: Machiavelli lists wars on Granada, Africa, Italy, and France. Ferdinand did not keep peace with his neighbors.

practice.hint: Machiavelli calls Ferdinand "the foremost king in Christendom." What does he say made Ferdinand so strong?

practice.stem: Machiavelli's way of judging Ferdinand's "pious cruelty" best reflects which of the following?

options.A: The belief that kings receive their power from God
options.B: The Christian humanist ideal of a prince who follows Christ
options.C: The idea that natural law limits what rulers may do
options.D: The view that results matter more than Christian morals

practice.explanation: Machiavelli calls the act "cruelty," yet he says it helped Ferdinand take on "still greater undertakings" and that no exploit "could be more wonderful or uncommon." He judges Ferdinand by what his actions achieved, not by Christian morals. This secular way of judging rulers shocked many of Machiavelli's readers.

whyNot.A: Thinkers such as Bossuet in the 1600s argued that kings rule by God's will. Machiavelli does not say God chose Ferdinand. He says Ferdinand used religion as a "cloak" and a "pretext."
whyNot.B: Christian humanists such as Erasmus urged princes to follow Christ's teachings and keep the peace. Machiavelli praises Ferdinand's wars. He does not condemn an act that he himself calls "cruelty."
whyNot.C: Natural-law thinkers such as Grotius later argued that some rules bind all rulers and nations. Machiavelli sets no such limits. He judges actions by whether they make a ruler stronger.

practice.hint: Machiavelli calls the act "cruelty." What does he seem to care about most when he judges Ferdinand?

practice.stem: Ferdinand's use of religion to strengthen royal power was most similar to which of the following?

options.A: Lorenzo de' Medici's support for artists and scholars in Florence
options.B: Henry VIII's making himself head of the Church of England
options.C: the Dutch revolt against the rule of the Spanish king Philip II
options.D: the Hanseatic League's control of trade in the Baltic Sea

practice.explanation: Like Ferdinand, Henry VIII used religion to gain power. The Act of Supremacy of 1534 made him head of the Church of England. It gave him control over the church's leaders and wealth.

whyNot.A: Lorenzo's patronage raised his prestige, but it was about art and learning, not about using religion to control his subjects.
whyNot.C: The Dutch revolt, which began in 1568, was a rebellion against a king, partly to protect Protestant worship. It weakened a monarch instead of strengthening him.
whyNot.D: The Hanseatic League was a group of merchant cities. It was about trade, not about a monarch's use of religion.

practice.hint: Look for another ruler who used religion to gain more control over his own kingdom.

practice.stem: According to the passage, the ideal courtier should

options.A: give up the practice of arms in order to spend his life in study
options.B: be both a skilled fighter and a well-read student of the humanities
options.C: study theology and church law so that he can serve as an adviser to the pope
options.D: write his poems and letters in Latin rather than in the everyday language

practice.explanation: Castiglione's courtier is skilled in both arms and letters. He reads the poets, orators, and historians of Greece and Rome, and he writes well in Italian.

whyNot.A: The speaker says the French are wrong to think that "letters are injurious to arms." He wants the courtier to be both a fighter and a scholar.
whyNot.C: The courtier studies poets, orators, and historians, not theology, and he serves a prince, not the pope.
whyNot.D: The speaker wants the courtier to write well "especially in this vulgar tongue of ours," meaning Italian.

practice.hint: Find what the speaker says about "letters" and about "arms."

practice.stem: The ideal described in the passage best illustrates which of the following?

options.A: The Renaissance ideal of the well-rounded individual
options.B: The monastic ideal of withdrawing from the world
options.C: The Protestant idea of salvation by faith alone
options.D: The scholastic method of defending Church teaching with logic

practice.explanation: Castiglione's courtier is good at many things. He can fight, read Latin and Greek, write poems, and speak well. This is the ideal of the well-rounded person. It was a secular model for how to live.

whyNot.B: Monks left the world to pray. The courtier lives at court, fights, and seeks "glory."
whyNot.C: Luther taught that people are saved by faith alone. The passage is about glory, learning, and skill, not salvation.
whyNot.D: Medieval scholastics used logic to explain Church teaching. The courtier studies poets, orators, and historians to win glory.

practice.hint: How many different skills does the speaker want the courtier to have?

practice.stem: The speaker's complaint that "the Italians have for some time since shown little martial valour" most likely refers to

options.A: the Ottoman conquest of Constantinople, a great Christian city, in 1453
options.B: the wars between Italian cities and Holy Roman emperors in the Middle Ages
options.C: the Hundred Years' War between England and France
options.D: the invasions of Italy by French and Spanish armies after 1494

practice.explanation: In 1494 the French king Charles VIII invaded Italy. French and Spanish armies then fought over Italy for decades. Italy's small states often lost to these big foreign armies. That embarrassed Italians like Castiglione.

whyNot.A: Constantinople fell to the Ottomans in 1453, decades before this book. The speaker means more recent defeats, when foreign armies invaded Italy itself after 1494.
whyNot.B: Italian cities fought the German emperors in the 1100s and 1200s, centuries before this book. The speaker says "for some time since," meaning recent years.
whyNot.C: The Hundred Years' War ended in 1453, decades before this book. The speaker means more recent defeats, when French and Spanish armies fought over Italy itself.

practice.hint: The book appeared in 1528. Which choice was still shaming Italian soldiers around that time?

practice.stem: Speaker B's main criticism is aimed at

options.A: Christians who pray directly to God instead of asking the saints to help them
options.B: sailors who ignore the orders of their ship's captain
options.C: Christians who read the Bible for themselves
options.D: practices, such as vows to saints, that turn faith into a business deal

practice.explanation: B says he does not "drive bargains with the saints." Some people promised candles or trips to shrines if a saint would help them. Erasmus thought this turned faith into a business deal.

whyNot.A: Speaker B prays directly to God himself: "I went immediately to the Father himself."
whyNot.B: The dialogue mentions the sailors only to show how they prayed. B does not blame them for disobeying orders.
whyNot.C: B judges the sailors' prayers by what "the holy scriptures" say. Erasmus wanted Christians to know the Bible better.

practice.hint: Why does speaker B refuse to make vows?

practice.stem: The ideas of speaker B best reflect which of the following?

options.A: Scholasticism
options.B: Christian humanism
options.C: Anabaptism
options.D: Philosophical skepticism

practice.explanation: Christian humanists such as Erasmus used Renaissance learning to call for church reform. They studied the Bible closely. They also made fun of practices they saw as superstition.

whyNot.A: Scholastics of the Middle Ages used logic to explain Church teachings. Erasmus mocked them and wanted a simpler faith based on the Bible.
whyNot.C: Anabaptists of the 1520s rejected infant baptism and formed separate churches. Erasmus stayed in the Catholic Church.
whyNot.D: Skeptics such as Montaigne doubted that people could know the truth for certain. B is sure that going straight to God is the right way to pray.

practice.hint: Look at the attribution. Who wrote the dialogue, and what kind of scholar was he?

practice.stem: In the long term, criticisms like those in the passage most directly contributed to

options.A: the Council of Trent's decision to end prayers to the saints
options.B: the Protestant Reformation's rejection of saints' shrines and pilgrimages
options.C: a growth in the number of pilgrims visiting English shrines such as Walsingham
options.D: the Baroque art that celebrated the saints in Catholic churches

practice.explanation: Erasmus stayed Catholic, but Protestant reformers used ideas like his. Reformers in Germany, Switzerland, and England attacked shrines, relics, and pilgrimages. People in his own time said that Erasmus laid the egg that Luther hatched.

whyNot.A: The Council of Trent (1545–1563) defended prayers to the saints and the honoring of relics.
whyNot.C: In 1538, during Henry VIII's break with Rome, the shrine at Walsingham was destroyed.
whyNot.D: Baroque art of the late 1500s and 1600s celebrated the saints to strengthen Catholic faith. It answered Protestant attacks; it did not grow out of Erasmus's criticism.

practice.hint: Check each choice: did it really happen, and did it attack or defend the honoring of saints?

practice.stem: According to the passage, enclosure harmed poor families mainly because

options.A: the king seized common lands to pay for his wars against France
options.B: the Church raised the tithes that peasants had to pay
options.C: town guilds kept the farm workers who lost their land from finding jobs in cities
options.D: landowners turned farmland into sheep pasture and evicted tenants

practice.explanation: More says landowners fenced in fields to keep sheep. Farm families lost their homes and their work. One shepherd could care for land that once needed many workers.

whyNot.A: The passage blames "the nobility and gentry" and the abbots, not the king.
whyNot.B: The passage does not mention tithes. It says the abbots, like other landlords, wanted more income from wool.
whyNot.C: The passage says there is no farm work left because "one shepherd" can do the work of many. It does not blame guilds.

practice.hint: Whom does More blame, and what did they do with the land?

practice.stem: The changes More describes are best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.A: The second serfdom in eastern Europe
options.B: The Agricultural Revolution of the 1700s
options.C: The commercialization of agriculture
options.D: The labor shortage after the Black Death

practice.explanation: English landowners had sold farm goods for centuries. In More's time, wool sold so well that some of them turned crop fields into sheep pasture. Farming more and more for sale in the market is called the commercialization of agriculture. It raised some landowners' profits but left many tenants without homes or work.

whyNot.A: In eastern Europe, nobles tied peasants more tightly to the land as serfs. In England, landlords pushed peasants off the land instead.
whyNot.B: More wrote in 1516, two centuries before the Agricultural Revolution of the 1700s.
whyNot.D: After the Black Death (1347–1351), workers were scarce and could demand more. More describes the opposite: too many workers and too few jobs.

practice.hint: Why did landowners want more wool? Think about selling to a market.

practice.stem: The problem of homeless poor people described in the passage contributed most directly to which later development in England?

options.A: The Elizabethan Poor Laws
options.B: The dissolution of the monasteries
options.C: The founding of the Bank of England
options.D: The Statute of Laborers

practice.explanation: Tudor governments worried about the growing number of poor and wandering people. The Poor Laws, especially the act of 1601, made each parish collect a tax for the poor. They also tried to put people who could work to work.

whyNot.B: Henry VIII closed the monasteries between 1536 and 1541 after his break with Rome. It was a religious and money-raising policy, and it actually removed a source of help for the poor.
whyNot.C: The Bank of England was founded in 1694 to lend money to the government, not to deal with poverty.
whyNot.D: The Statute of Laborers (1351) tried to hold down wages after the Black Death, long before More wrote.

practice.hint: Check the date of each choice. Which one came after 1516 and dealt with the poor?

practice.stem: The painting's subject best reflects which feature of Northern Renaissance art?

options.A: scenes from the myths of ancient Greek and Roman gods
options.B: dramatic religious scenes meant to strengthen Catholic faith
options.C: an interest in the everyday lives of ordinary people
options.D: idealized portraits of kings and popes

practice.explanation: Northern Renaissance artists such as Bruegel painted ordinary people and daily life in great detail. Here peasants cut wheat, eat, and rest during the harvest.

whyNot.A: Italian Renaissance artists often painted ancient myths. Bruegel shows peasants at work, with no gods in sight.
whyNot.B: Dramatic religious scenes were typical of Baroque art in the 1600s. This painting shows farm work, not a religious story.
whyNot.D: The people in the painting are peasants, not rulers or popes.

practice.hint: Who are the people in the painting, and what are they doing?

practice.stem: Which feature of rural life in the 1500s is most clearly illustrated by the painting?

options.A: Farm families worked mainly at making cloth for merchants.
options.B: Landowners had turned grain fields into pasture for sheep.
options.C: Farm work followed the seasons and depended on human labor.
options.D: Peasants in the Low Countries were bound to the land as serfs.

practice.explanation: Workers cut and bundle the wheat by hand at harvest time, then rest and eat in the field. Bruegel painted this scene as one of a series showing the work of each time of year. Most Europeans lived by farming, and the seasons set the pattern of their work.

whyNot.A: Some rural families did spin and weave cloth for merchants, but these workers are harvesting grain, not making cloth.
whyNot.B: Some English landowners did turn fields into sheep pasture, but this painting shows a field full of wheat.
whyNot.D: Nothing in the painting shows serfdom. Serfdom was spreading in eastern Europe, but most peasants in the Low Countries were free and paid rent.

practice.hint: Look at the workers' tools and the crop they are gathering. What time of year is it?

practice.stem: The fact that the painting was owned by a rich Antwerp merchant best illustrates which development?

options.A: the Catholic Church's control over art in the Low Countries
options.B: the decline of Antwerp as a center of trade in the 1560s
options.C: the end of the guilds in the cities of Flanders
options.D: the rise of merchants as major buyers of art

practice.explanation: Antwerp was a center of world trade in the 1500s. Wealthy merchants like Niclaes Jonghelinck spent their money on art for their homes. This new commercial elite became an important group of patrons, alongside nobles and the Church.

whyNot.A: This painting was made for a merchant's house, not a church. Merchants were becoming major buyers of art.
whyNot.B: In the 1560s Antwerp was still one of Europe's richest trading cities. It declined after Spanish troops took it in 1585 and the Dutch closed its river to ships.
whyNot.C: Guilds stayed powerful in Flemish cities through the 1500s and long after.

practice.hint: Who paid for most art in earlier centuries, and who is paying for it here?

practice.stem: In Source 1, Caxton's main reason for printing the book was that

options.A: printing let him make many copies at once
options.B: the Duke of Burgundy had ordered him to set up a press
options.C: printed books lasted longer than books written on parchment
options.D: the Church had asked him to print copies of the Bible

practice.explanation: Caxton's hand and eyes were tired from copying by hand. With a press, he could make many copies at the same time. When he says all the copies "were begun in one day, and also finished in one day," he means they were made together, not one after another. The printing job itself took much longer than one day.

whyNot.B: Caxton says he learned printing "at my great charge and dispense," meaning at his own cost. He does not say anyone ordered him to print.
whyNot.C: Caxton never compares how long books last. His point is speed: he is tired of writing by hand.
whyNot.D: The book is a story of Troy, not the Bible.

practice.hint: What problems with writing by hand does Caxton describe?

practice.stem: Caxton's problem in Source 2 best illustrates the connection between printing and which of the following?

options.A: The growth of national languages and literatures
options.B: The humanist revival of classical Latin among scholars
options.C: The decline of the English cloth trade
options.D: The scholastic method in the universities

practice.explanation: English was spoken differently from shire to shire. Printers like Caxton had to pick one way to write it. Over time, printing in everyday languages helped create standard national languages and literatures.

whyNot.B: Humanists did revive classical Latin, but Caxton's problem is how to write English so that all English readers can understand it.
whyNot.C: The merchants in the story were traveling to trade, but Caxton's point is about words, not about cloth.
whyNot.D: Scholastic teachers wrote and taught in Latin. Caxton is choosing words for English readers.

practice.hint: Caxton must choose between "eggs" and "eyren." Why does a printer have to choose?

practice.stem: Taken together, the two sources best support which conclusion?

options.A: Early printing in England was controlled by the Catholic Church.
options.B: Caxton printed mainly religious works for the clergy.
options.C: Printing in English began in England before it began on the Continent.
options.D: Early printers sold books in everyday languages to a growing number of readers.

practice.explanation: Caxton printed stories in English for buyers who were not scholars. He wanted words that "common people" could understand. Printing was creating a market for books in everyday languages.

whyNot.A: Caxton made his own choices about what to print and how to write it. Nothing in either source shows Church control.
whyNot.B: Both books Caxton describes are stories of ancient Troy and Rome, put into English for "gentlemen" and "common people."
whyNot.C: The attribution says Caxton printed Source 1 at Bruges, in the Low Countries, about 1474. He set up his press in England only in 1476.

practice.hint: Who were Caxton's readers, and in what language did he print for them?

practice.stem: The title and the two portraits at the top of the map suggest that the mapmakers

options.A: replaced ancient Greek geography with teachings from the Bible
options.B: relied mainly on Chinese maps of the Pacific Ocean
options.C: combined ancient geographic knowledge with information from recent voyages
options.D: wanted to honor the Spanish and Portuguese monarchs who had paid for the voyages

practice.explanation: Ptolemy stands for the old Greek geography that Renaissance scholars found again. Vespucci stands for new knowledge from Atlantic voyages. The map joins the two.

whyNot.A: The title says the map follows the "tradition" of Ptolemy, an ancient Greek geographer. It does not replace his geography with teachings from the Bible.
whyNot.B: The title credits Ptolemy, Vespucci, and other voyagers, not Chinese mapmakers.
whyNot.D: The title and the two portraits honor a geographer and a navigator, not the monarchs who paid for the voyages.

practice.hint: Who are the two men at the top, and what does each one stand for?

practice.stem: The way this map was produced most directly affected European exploration by

options.A: giving navigators a reliable way to measure longitude at sea
options.B: spreading news of recent voyages to readers across Europe
options.C: settling disputes between Spain and Portugal over new lands
options.D: helping rulers keep the routes of their voyages secret

practice.explanation: The map was printed from carved woodblocks, so many copies could be made and sold. Printed maps and books spread news of the voyages, and the new name "America," across Europe.

whyNot.A: Printing made copies of maps. It did not solve the problem of finding longitude at sea, which was solved only in the 1700s with accurate clocks.
whyNot.C: Spain and Portugal settled their claims by treaties, such as the Treaty of Tordesillas in 1494. A printed map did not settle them.
whyNot.D: Printing did the opposite. Many printed copies made news of the voyages harder to keep secret.

practice.hint: How is printing a map different from drawing it by hand?

practice.stem: The name printed on the land at the far left suggests that, by 1507, some Europeans

options.A: saw the lands across the Atlantic as a new continent and not as part of Asia
options.B: accepted Columbus's claim that he had reached the coast of Asia
options.C: knew that Spain had already conquered both the Aztec and the Inca empires
options.D: believed the new lands had first been reached by Viking sailors

practice.explanation: Amerigo Vespucci wrote that the lands he explored were a new world. The mapmakers agreed. They drew a separate land with an ocean between it and Asia and named it America after him.

whyNot.B: Columbus claimed that the lands he reached were part of Asia. The mapmakers drew a separate land, with an ocean between it and Asia, and named it for Vespucci instead.
whyNot.C: Spain conquered the Aztecs in 1521 and the Incas in the 1530s, years after this map was printed.
whyNot.D: Norse sailors did reach North America around the year 1000, but nothing on the map points to them. Its title and portraits credit Ptolemy and recent voyagers such as Vespucci.

practice.hint: Columbus thought he had reached Asia. Whom did the mapmakers name the land after, and how did they draw it?

practice.stem: Raleigh's main argument is that Spain's power in Europe

options.A: came from its exports of wine, oranges, and other farm goods
options.B: rested on the gold and silver it took from its colonies in the Americas
options.C: depended on its alliance with England against their common enemies
options.D: had ended when its fleet was defeated in 1588

practice.explanation: Raleigh says Spain's "Indian gold" pays for its armies and its bribes. That gold threatens every other country in Europe. He hopes England can find its own treasure in Guiana.

whyNot.A: Raleigh says Spain's strength does not come from "the trades of sacks and Seville oranges."
whyNot.C: Raleigh treats Spain as a dangerous rival. England and Spain were at war when he wrote.
whyNot.D: Raleigh says the Spanish king "repaired" his losses of 1588 and is still powerful.

practice.hint: What does Raleigh say Spain's power does not come from, and what does it come from?

practice.stem: Raleigh's argument is best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.A: The Thirty Years' War in the German states
options.B: The Wars of the Roses between English nobles
options.C: England's long war with Spain under Elizabeth I
options.D: The Italian Wars between France and Spain

practice.explanation: England and Spain were at war from 1585 to 1604. Raleigh mentions the Armada of 1588 ("Eighty-eight") and wants England to win treasure that would weaken Spain.

whyNot.A: The Thirty Years' War began in 1618, more than twenty years after Raleigh wrote.
whyNot.B: The Wars of the Roses were fought between English noble families from 1455 to 1485.
whyNot.D: The Italian Wars were fought mainly by France and Spain over Italy, and they ended in 1559.

practice.hint: Raleigh mentions "Eighty-eight," the year 1588. What was happening between England and Spain at that time?

practice.stem: In the 1600s, English efforts like the one Raleigh proposed led most directly to

options.A: the English conquest of Spain's silver mines in Peru
options.B: English control of the spice trade of the East Indies
options.C: a lasting alliance between England and Spain against the Dutch
options.D: English colonies in North America and the Caribbean

practice.explanation: Raleigh's Guiana plan failed, but England kept trying. In the 1600s it founded Virginia (1607) and Barbados (1627). England joined France and the Dutch in challenging Spain and Portugal overseas.

whyNot.A: England never conquered Peru. Spain kept its silver mines there until the 1800s.
whyNot.B: The Dutch, not the English, controlled most of the spice trade of the East Indies in the 1600s.
whyNot.C: England and Spain made peace in 1604, but they stayed rivals for colonies and trade.

practice.hint: Raleigh never found the gold of Guiana. Where did the English set up colonies instead?

practice.stem: Which of the following best describes a difference between the two sources?

options.A: Columbus describes the islanders as fierce warriors, while Montaigne describes the Brazilians as a peaceful people.
options.B: Columbus criticizes Spanish cruelty, while Montaigne defends the cruelty of Europeans.
options.C: Columbus relies on books he has read, while Montaigne relies on his own visit to Brazil.
options.D: Columbus sees the islanders as useful to Spain, while Montaigne questions calling other peoples barbarous.

practice.explanation: Columbus sees the Taíno as future "servants" and Christians, and he looks for gold. Montaigne says people call anything "barbarism" if it is not done in their own country.

whyNot.A: Columbus says the islanders are "very simple as regards the use of arms." Montaigne writes about a people who kill prisoners of war.
whyNot.B: Columbus says "fifty men" could conquer the islanders, and Montaigne condemns cruelty done "under colour of piety and religion."
whyNot.C: Columbus describes what he saw himself. Montaigne never went to Brazil; he learned about it from others.

practice.hint: What does each writer want or argue? Compare their purposes.

practice.stem: Source 1 provides evidence for which motives for European exploration?

options.A: Escape from religious persecution in their home countries
options.B: The search for gold and the spread of Christianity
options.C: Relief from crowded European cities
options.D: The scientific study of plants and animals

practice.explanation: Columbus searches for gold. He also says the islanders "would easily be made Christians." Gold, God, and glory for the crown drove many explorers.

whyNot.A: Groups like the English Pilgrims later sailed to escape persecution (1620). Columbus sailed for the Spanish crown to find riches and new lands.
whyNot.C: Spain's rulers paid for the voyage to find wealth and a route to Asia, not to move extra people overseas.
whyNot.D: Columbus does not describe plants or animals in this passage. He takes "trouble to ascertain if there was gold."

practice.hint: What does Columbus try to find out, and what does he say about the islanders' religion?

practice.stem: Montaigne's mention of cruelty "among neighbours and fellow-citizens" done "under colour of piety and religion" most likely refers to

options.A: The Spanish conquest of the Aztecs
options.B: The Hundred Years' War
options.C: The Thirty Years' War
options.D: The French Wars of Religion

practice.explanation: From 1562 to 1598, French Catholics and Protestants (Huguenots) fought a series of civil wars. Montaigne lived through massacres such as St. Bartholomew's Day in 1572, so he could say he had "lately seen" such cruelty.

whyNot.A: The Spanish conquest took place in Mexico, among peoples who were not Montaigne's neighbors and fellow citizens.
whyNot.B: The Hundred Years' War was fought between the English and the French and ended in 1453. It was not a war over religion.
whyNot.C: The Thirty Years' War began in 1618, after Montaigne's death in 1592.

practice.hint: Montaigne was French and wrote in 1580. What was happening in France at that time?

practice.stem: The changes Garcilaso describes are best understood as part of which of the following?

options.A: The Columbian Exchange
options.B: The price revolution
options.C: The Commercial Revolution in banking
options.D: The Reconquista

practice.explanation: After 1492, plants, animals, and diseases moved between Europe and the Americas. Horses, cattle, pigs, wheat, grapes, and sugar cane came to the Americas. Maize and potatoes went to Europe.

whyNot.B: The price revolution was the rise of prices in Europe in the 1500s. Garcilaso describes animals and plants coming to Peru.
whyNot.C: Banking changes such as double-entry bookkeeping happened in European cities. Garcilaso writes about horses, cattle, wheat, and sugar in Peru.
whyNot.D: The Reconquista was the Christian conquest of Muslim Spain, completed in 1492. It did not move plants and animals across the Atlantic.

practice.hint: Where did the animals and plants Garcilaso lists come from, and where did they go?

practice.stem: Garcilaso's background most likely shaped his account in which of the following ways?

options.A: He wanted to persuade the Spanish king to return Peru to Inca rule.
options.B: He had not seen Spanish farm animals until he moved to Spain.
options.C: He could report Indigenous people's reactions as well as Spanish actions.
options.D: He wanted to prove that European crops could not grow in the Andes.

practice.explanation: Garcilaso's mother was an Inca noblewoman, and his father was a Spanish conquistador. He grew up in Cuzco. So he could describe the Spaniards' new animals and also the crowds of Native people who came to stare at them.

whyNot.A: Garcilaso praises the Spaniards' "diligence" and does not call for an end to Spanish rule in this passage.
whyNot.B: Garcilaso says he saw the first bullocks plowing in Cuzco around 1550, when he was a boy in Peru.
whyNot.D: Garcilaso says Spanish crops now grow in "such abundance" that they are "held very cheap."

practice.hint: Think about the people Garcilaso grew up among. Whose reactions does he describe in the second paragraph?

practice.stem: The "sugar estates" Garcilaso mentions are most closely connected to which development in the Atlantic world?

options.A: the growth of sugar estates worked mainly by Native laborers who were paid wages
options.B: a fall in European demand for sugar
options.C: the growth of plantations worked by enslaved Africans
options.D: a shift from enslaved Africans to European indentured servants on sugar plantations

practice.explanation: Growing sugar took huge amounts of hard work. Disease and forced labor killed many Indigenous people. So colonists in Brazil, the Caribbean, and Peru turned to enslaved Africans.

whyNot.A: Some Native people did work for wages, but disease and forced labor had killed many of them. Sugar estates came to rely more and more on enslaved Africans.
whyNot.B: European demand for sugar grew quickly in the 1500s and 1600s.
whyNot.D: The change went the other way. In English Barbados, beginning in the 1640s, sugar planters replaced most of their indentured servants from Europe with enslaved Africans.

practice.hint: Think about what sugar plantations needed most besides land.

practice.stem: The account treats the captured Africans mainly as

options.A: converts to be taught the Christian faith
options.B: soldiers to help fight the Spanish in Hispaniola
options.C: free workers hired for wages in the Caribbean
options.D: goods to be seized and sold for profit

practice.explanation: The account calls the captured Africans "very good merchandise." It lists them with "other merchandises." Hawkins and his investors made "much gain" by selling them.

whyNot.A: The account never mentions religion. It calls the captives "merchandise" and "prey."
whyNot.B: Hawkins sold the captives to Spanish colonists. He did not use them as soldiers.
whyNot.C: The captives were taken "by the sword" and sold. They were not hired for wages.

practice.hint: What words does the account use for the people Hawkins captured?

practice.stem: Hawkins's belief that enslaved Africans "were very good merchandise in Hispaniola" is best explained by which of the following?

options.A: the collapse of the Native population and the growth of sugar farming
options.B: a law of Philip II that invited English merchants to supply the Spanish colonies
options.C: the end of the Portuguese slave trade after the Treaty of Tordesillas
options.D: the discovery of rich silver mines on Hispaniola

practice.explanation: Disease, war, and forced labor killed most of the Taíno people of Hispaniola after 1492. Spanish colonists needed workers for sugar mills and cattle ranches. So enslaved Africans sold for high prices.

whyNot.B: Philip II did not invite English traders. Spain required royal permission to trade with its colonies, and some foreign merchants did get licenses, but Hawkins had no license from the Spanish crown. That is why he trusted the Spaniards only as far as "his own strength" could "master them."
whyNot.C: The Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) put Africa on Portugal's side of the line. The Portuguese slave trade kept growing after it.
whyNot.D: Spain's great silver mines were in Mexico and Peru, not on Hispaniola.

practice.hint: What had happened to the Native people of Hispaniola since 1492?

practice.stem: Voyages like Hawkins's contributed most directly to which of the following?

options.A: The union of the Spanish and Portuguese crowns
options.B: The Treaty of Tordesillas
options.C: Rising conflict between England and Spain
options.D: The Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire

practice.explanation: Spain claimed the right to control all trade with its colonies. English traders and raiders like Hawkins and Drake broke that rule, which angered Philip II. The rivalry helped lead to war in 1585 and the Spanish Armada of 1588.

whyNot.A: Philip II became king of Portugal in 1580 because the Portuguese royal line died out, not because of English voyages.
whyNot.B: The Treaty of Tordesillas was signed in 1494, almost seventy years before Hawkins's voyage.
whyNot.D: Pizarro conquered the Incas in the 1530s, before Hawkins sailed.

practice.hint: How would the king of Spain feel about English ships trading in his colonies without permission?

practice.stem: According to Pacioli, the most important thing a merchant needs is

options.A: a license from the duke
options.B: cash or good credit
options.C: a partner in Venice
options.D: a blessing from a priest

practice.explanation: Pacioli lists three things a merchant needs. He says the most important is cash or something worth the same. A merchant with good credit could also do big business.

whyNot.A: Pacioli mentions the Duke of Urbino only because he wrote the book for the duke's subjects.
whyNot.C: Pacioli recommends the bookkeeping system "used in Venice," not a Venetian partner.
whyNot.D: Pacioli compares a merchant's credit to Christian faith, but he does not say a merchant needs a priest's blessing.

practice.hint: Pacioli lists three things. Which one does he call "the most important"?

practice.stem: Pacioli's treatise is best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.A: Stricter guild rules controlling the training of urban craftspeople
options.B: Lords' growing demands for labor from peasants in eastern Europe
options.C: Church efforts to limit the interest charged on loans
options.D: The growth of banking and long-distance trade in Italian cities

practice.explanation: Venice, Florence, and Genoa were centers of banking and trade. Their merchants used double-entry bookkeeping. Pacioli's printed book explained the Venetian way of keeping accounts.

whyNot.A: Guilds trained craftspeople such as weavers and goldsmiths. Pacioli writes for merchants about cash, credit, and keeping accounts.
whyNot.B: In eastern Europe, lords were demanding more labor from their peasants. Pacioli writes about merchants in the trading cities of Italy.
whyNot.C: The Church did condemn charging interest, which it called usury, but Pacioli does not discuss interest. He explains how merchants should keep their accounts.

practice.hint: Pacioli praises merchants' credit and the way of keeping accounts "used in Venice." What kind of business needed such careful records?

practice.stem: Pacioli's statement that "in the great republics nothing was considered superior to the word of the good merchant" best reflects which of the following?

options.A: the control of trade by noble landowners in eastern Europe
options.B: the decline of the guilds in Italian cities
options.C: the power of merchant families in Italian city-states
options.D: the merchants' loss of power to the Catholic Church

practice.explanation: In Venice, Florence, and Genoa, rich merchant and banking families such as the Medici held great political power. Their wealth and good name made them leaders of their cities.

whyNot.A: In eastern Europe, nobles ran great estates worked by serfs. Pacioli is writing about the Italian republics.
whyNot.B: Guilds remained important in Italian cities. Pacioli is praising merchants' honesty, not describing guilds.
whyNot.D: Pacioli describes merchants whose word was trusted above everything, not merchants losing power.

practice.hint: Who ran "the great republics" of Renaissance Italy?

practice.stem: Which of the following best describes Lea's main argument?

options.A: Ferdinand and Isabella built royal power mainly through the Hermandad, not the Inquisition.
options.B: Ferdinand and Isabella used the Inquisition as their main weapon against the nobles.
options.C: The towns of Castile kept their independence by allying with the nobles against the crown.
options.D: The popes blocked Ferdinand's efforts to take control of the military orders.

practice.explanation: Lea says the Hermandad, a royal police force, made the crown strong. Royal control of the rich military orders helped too. He rejects the idea that the Inquisition was the main cause.

whyNot.B: Lea says, "He reads history to little purpose who imagines that this was the work of the Inquisition."
whyNot.C: Lea says the Hermandad was "an alliance between the crown and the people" against "the centrifugal forces of feudalism," meaning the power of the nobles.
whyNot.D: Lea says the crown achieved "the virtual incorporation" of the orders' masterships, a step in "establishing the royal supremacy." He does not say the popes blocked it. In fact, popes allowed Ferdinand to run the orders.

practice.hint: What institutions does Lea say did the most to centralize power?

practice.stem: The developments Lea describes best illustrate which of the following?

options.A: The growth of parliamentary limits on royal power
options.B: The new monarchies' centralization of power
options.C: The political fragmentation of the Holy Roman Empire
options.D: The rise of republican government in Italian city-states

practice.explanation: New monarchs built armies, collected taxes, and took control of courts. Examples are Ferdinand and Isabella in Spain, Henry VII in England, and Louis XI in France. These steps laid the base for the modern state.

whyNot.A: In England, Parliament gained power over kings mainly in the 1600s. Lea describes a Spanish crown that became "absolute."
whyNot.C: The Holy Roman Empire stayed divided among hundreds of princes and cities. Lea describes royal power growing stronger in Spain.
whyNot.D: Republics such as Venice and Florence were governed by councils of leading citizens. Lea describes a king and queen gaining power.

practice.hint: Did royal power in Spain grow or shrink in Lea's account?

practice.stem: Ferdinand's control of the military orders was most similar to which of the following?

options.A: The English Parliament's Petition of Right
options.B: The French king's control of bishops' posts under the Concordat of Bologna
options.C: The election of the Holy Roman Emperor by seven princes
options.D: The Dutch East India Company's right to make war and treaties in Asia

practice.explanation: In the Concordat of Bologna (1516), the pope let the French king name the bishops and abbots of France. Like Ferdinand with the military orders, the king gained control of rich and powerful church posts.

whyNot.A: The Petition of Right (1628) limited the English king's power. Ferdinand's control of the orders increased his power.
whyNot.C: Seven princes chose the emperor, under rules confirmed by the Golden Bull of 1356. That gave the princes power over the emperor. It is the opposite of Ferdinand's gain.
whyNot.D: The Dutch East India Company's powers (1602) were given by the Dutch government to a trading company. They did not increase a king's power.

practice.hint: What did Ferdinand gain when he took over the military orders? Look for another ruler who gained the same kind of control.

exam.title: Unit 1 Practice Exam: Renaissance and Exploration
exam.directions: Each set of questions refers to a source: a primary source, a historian's writing, an image, or data. For each question, choose the best answer. Use the source and your knowledge of European history from c. 1450 to c. 1648. There is no penalty for guessing. Some sources use historical labels or words for groups of people that are no longer used; these words show the language of their time.

questions.stem: Burckhardt's argument emphasizes which of the following as the main cause of the developments he describes?

options.A: The political circumstances of the Italian states
options.B: The spread of the printing press across Europe
options.C: The wealth that Europe gained from the Atlantic trade
options.D: The teachings of the medieval Catholic Church

rationales.A: Correct. Burckhardt says the result "was owing above all to the political circumstances of Italy," with its republics and despotisms.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Burckhardt dates the change to "the close of the thirteenth century," long before printing began in Europe in the 1450s.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The Atlantic trade grew after 1500, long after the change Burckhardt dates to the late 1200s and 1300s.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Burckhardt says the medieval "veil" was "woven of faith, illusion, and childish prepossession," and that it melted away in Italy.

questions.explanation: Burckhardt says Italy's many states, whether republics or ruled by despots, shaped its people. In such states, people began to see themselves as individuals.

questions.stem: A historian who wished to qualify Burckhardt's argument would most likely point to which of the following?

options.A: Italian rulers paid artists to paint portraits that celebrated their own achievements.
options.B: Italian humanists such as Pico della Mirandola praised human dignity and potential.
options.C: Machiavelli judged rulers by whether their actions worked rather than by Christian morals.
options.D: Medieval writers such as Peter Abelard described their own experiences and inner lives.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Portraits that praised rulers support Burckhardt. He says despotism made the ruler himself a strong individual.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Pico's praise of human dignity and abilities, in 1486, supports Burckhardt's picture of Italians who saw themselves as individuals.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Machiavelli's secular view of politics supports Burckhardt. He says people began to look at "the state" in a new, "objective" way.
rationales.D: Correct. Burckhardt says that in the Middle Ages "man was conscious of himself only as member of a race, people, party, family, or corporation." Abelard's story of his own life, written in the 1100s, shows that some medieval people already wrote about themselves as individuals.

questions.explanation: To qualify an argument is to show its limits. Burckhardt says medieval people saw themselves only as members of groups. Medieval writers who described their own lives and feelings show that a strong sense of self did not begin only in Renaissance Italy.

questions.stem: Which of the following would best support Burckhardt's claim about individuality in Renaissance Italy?

options.A: Italian artists such as Benvenuto Cellini wrote about their own lives and talents.
options.B: Italian city-states stopped hiring mercenary captains as wars among them came to an end.
options.C: Italian guilds gained tighter control over how their members dressed and worked.
options.D: Italian humanists rejected Greek and Roman writers as pagans.

rationales.A: Correct. Cellini wrote a famous autobiography in the 1550s and 1560s that boasts of his own talents and deeds. Such life stories show the pride in the self that Burckhardt describes.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Wars among the Italian states continued, and rulers kept hiring condottieri, commanders of hired soldiers.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Tighter guild control would show people living as members of a "corporation," which is how Burckhardt describes the Middle Ages.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Italian humanists admired Greek and Roman writers and worked hard to recover their texts.

questions.explanation: Burckhardt says that in the Middle Ages people saw themselves only as members of a group. An artist's life story that celebrates his own talents shows a new pride in the self.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a difference between the two sources?

options.A: Source 1 opens the oceans to the Christian rulers of Europe, while Source 2 limits them to the Dutch.
options.B: Source 1 divides new lands between two crowns, while Source 2 defends the right of every nation to trade freely.
options.C: Source 1 bases its claims on the law of nations, while Source 2 bases its claims on a gift from the pope.
options.D: Source 1 assigns territory by a negotiated boundary, while Source 2 assigns trading rights according to earlier voyages.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Source 1 gives lands to Portugal and Castile alone, and Grotius says the right "belongs equally to all nations."
rationales.B: Correct. Source 1 draws a line "from pole to pole" and gives the lands on each side to Portugal or to Castile. Grotius says, "Every nation is free to travel to every other nation, and to trade with it."
rationales.C: Incorrect. Grotius, not the treaty, appeals to the "Law of Nations." The treaty is an agreement between two sets of rulers, and Grotius does not rest his case on the pope.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The treaty does set a boundary, but Grotius says the right to trade "belongs equally to all nations." He does not give it to whoever sailed a route first.

questions.explanation: The treaty split newly found lands between Portugal and Castile. Grotius argued that no nation could stop others from sailing the seas and trading.

questions.stem: Source 2 is best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.A: Spanish efforts to conquer the Aztec Empire
options.B: English searches for a northwest passage to China
options.C: Dutch competition with Portugal for the spice trade of Asia
options.D: Venetian wars with the Ottoman Empire for control of the Mediterranean

rationales.A: Incorrect. The Spanish conquered the Aztecs in 1521, almost a century earlier, and Grotius writes about the East Indies.
rationales.B: Incorrect. English explorers did search for a northwest passage, but Grotius defends Dutch voyages to the East Indies.
rationales.C: Correct. Around 1600 Dutch ships began sailing to the East Indies, where Portugal had long claimed control of the spice trade. Grotius defended the Dutch right to trade there.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Venice fought the Ottomans in the Mediterranean, but Grotius is writing about the Dutch and the open ocean.

questions.explanation: The Dutch were at war with Spain, whose king also ruled Portugal from 1580 to 1640. When Dutch merchants began trading in Asia, the Portuguese claimed the right to keep them out. Grotius answered that the seas were open to all.

questions.stem: The provisions in the second paragraph of Source 1 most directly reflect which of the following?

options.A: European use of gunpowder weapons to seize land overseas
options.B: European use of joint-stock companies to raise money for long ocean voyages
options.C: European efforts to reach Asian markets by sailing around Africa
options.D: European use of new ways to find a ship's position at sea

rationales.A: Incorrect. The paragraph describes measuring and mapping, not fighting.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Large joint-stock companies such as the English and Dutch East India Companies were founded around 1600, about a century after this treaty. These caravels were to be sent by the two monarchs.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Portugal did seek a sea route to Asia around Africa, but this paragraph plans a joint survey to mark the boundary line in the Atlantic.
rationales.D: Correct. The treaty sends pilots and others to study "the degrees of the sun or of north latitude." Sailors used instruments such as the astrolabe and the quadrant to measure the height of the sun and find their latitude.

questions.explanation: To draw the line, sailors had to know where they were at sea. New skills and tools for measuring latitude, along with better maps, made long ocean voyages possible.

questions.stem: Grotius most likely wrote Source 2 to defend the activities of which of the following?

options.A: The merchants of the Hanseatic League
options.B: The Spanish treasure fleets from America
options.C: The Dutch East India Company
options.D: The Medici Bank of Florence

rationales.A: Incorrect. The Hanseatic League was a group of German trading cities on the Baltic and North Seas, not in the East Indies.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The Spanish treasure fleets carried American silver to Spain. Grotius defends the Dutch, who were at war with Spain.
rationales.C: Correct. The Dutch East India Company, founded in 1602, traded and fought in Asia. Grotius first wrote this argument for the company after Dutch ships seized a Portuguese ship, the Santa Catarina, in 1603.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The Medici Bank was a Florentine bank of the 1400s. It had collapsed long before 1609.

questions.explanation: Grotius says the Dutch "have the right to sail to the East Indies" and trade there. This defended the Dutch East India Company. It was a joint-stock company that became one of the richest businesses in Europe.

questions.stem: The painting's lifelike detail in the people, cloth, and objects best reflects which artistic development?

options.A: Northern Renaissance naturalism
options.B: The Italian revival of classical myths
options.C: Protestant destruction of religious images
options.D: Fresco painting on the walls of churches

rationales.A: Correct. Northern painters such as Holbein, Jan van Eyck, and Bruegel painted people and objects in exact, lifelike detail.
