rationales.B: Incorrect. Italian artists such as Botticelli painted scenes from Greek and Roman myths. This painting shows two real men of the 1530s and real objects, not gods or heroes.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Some Protestants in the 1520s and 1530s removed or smashed religious images in churches. That explains a loss of religious art, not Holbein's fine, lifelike detail.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Fresco is painting on wet plaster, used on the walls of Italian churches and palaces. The Ambassadors is an oil painting on wooden panels, and oil paint let Northern artists show very fine detail.

questions.explanation: Holbein paints fur, silk, a carpet, and scientific tools so exactly that they look real. Careful, lifelike detail, often done in oil paint, was a mark of Northern Renaissance art.

questions.stem: The globe and instruments on the top level of the table are most closely connected to which development of the period?

options.A: advances in astronomy and the science of navigation at sea
options.B: the invention of printing with movable type in Germany
options.C: the use of gunpowder weapons in siege warfare
options.D: the development of double-entry bookkeeping in Italy

rationales.A: Correct. Instruments such as the quadrant measured the height of the sun and stars. Sailors used such tools, along with better maps and globes, to find their way at sea.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Printing appears in the painting through the books on the lower level, not the instruments on the top level.
rationales.C: Incorrect. None of these objects is a weapon. They measure time and the positions of the sun and stars.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Bookkeeping was a method of keeping business records, not something done with globes and quadrants.

questions.explanation: The globes and tools show a new interest in the stars and the shape of the world. The same knowledge helped sailors cross oceans in the Age of Exploration.

questions.stem: The books on the lower level, an arithmetic book for merchants and a hymnbook, best reflect which of the following?

options.A: the continued production of luxury manuscripts for courtly patrons
options.B: the expansion of university teaching in Latin theology
options.C: the collection of Greek and Roman manuscripts by humanist scholars
options.D: the spread of printed books on practical and religious subjects

rationales.A: Incorrect. Some rich patrons still ordered handwritten luxury books, but an arithmetic book for merchants and a hymnbook for singing in church were everyday books. The two books in the painting were printed in Germany in the 1520s.
rationales.B: Incorrect. These books teach arithmetic and hymns for worship. They are not works of Latin theology for university students.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Humanists did collect ancient Greek and Roman texts, but these books are about business math and Christian worship.
rationales.D: Correct. By the 1530s, printers turned out many books on practical subjects such as arithmetic, along with hymnbooks and Bibles.

questions.explanation: Printing made books cheaper and more common. Merchants bought books that taught arithmetic, and Protestant churches printed hymnbooks so that people could sing in their own language.

questions.stem: During the period 1495 to 1593, the major factor explaining the trend shown in the table was that

options.A: a shortage of workers after the Black Death forced landowners to raise wages
options.B: rising population and American silver pushed food prices up faster than wages
options.C: new crops from the Americas, such as the potato, flooded English markets with cheap food
options.D: Parliament required local officials to raise wages each year to keep up with food prices

rationales.A: Incorrect. The Black Death struck in the 1300s, and higher wages would have meant fewer weeks of work, not more.
rationales.B: Correct. In the 1500s Europe's population grew back to its level before the Black Death, and silver from Spanish America flowed into Europe. Prices, especially for food, rose faster than wages. Historians call this the price revolution.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Potatoes were not widely grown in England until much later, and cheap food would have lowered the weeks needed, not raised them.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Local officials set the highest wages that workers could be paid, and those wages did not keep up with prices, as the rising number of weeks shows.

questions.explanation: In Rogers's estimates, a craftsman needed 10 weeks of work to buy his family's grain in 1495 and 40 weeks in 1593. Wages rose slowly while grain prices rose quickly, so working people grew poorer.

questions.stem: The trend shown in the table most directly contributed to which of the following in England?

options.A: the binding of English peasants to the land as serfs
options.B: more poverty and vagrancy, which led to new poor laws
options.C: the end of the enclosure of farmland by landowners
options.D: a steady decline in the population of London

rationales.A: Incorrect. Serfdom was growing in eastern Europe, but English peasants were becoming free tenants and wage workers.
rationales.B: Correct. As food took more and more of their wages, many workers fell into poverty. Parliament passed poor laws, such as the act of 1601, that made each parish help its poor.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Rising food prices made farming for the market more profitable, and enclosure continued.
rationales.D: Incorrect. London grew quickly in the 1500s and early 1600s as poor people from the countryside moved there to look for work.

questions.explanation: At the 1593 wage rates Rogers used, a farm laborer could not buy his family's grain even with a full year of work. Poverty spread, and the government tried to respond with poor laws.

questions.stem: Valla's method in the last paragraph best illustrates which of the following?

options.A: Humanist philology
options.B: Scholastic theology
options.C: Divine-right absolutism
options.D: Christian mysticism

rationales.A: Correct. Philology is the study of how language is used in old texts. Valla argues that the word "satraps" does not fit the government of Constantine's Rome. He tests the document against the language and history of the time it claims to come from.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Scholastic theologians used logic to explain Christian teachings. Valla tests a document by studying its language.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Divine-right absolutism is the belief that kings get their power from God. Valla is studying the words of an old document.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Mystics sought a direct experience of God through prayer. Valla's argument is about Latin words and Roman history.

questions.explanation: Humanists knew old Latin and Roman history very well. They could spot words that did not belong in an old text. Valla used this skill to show that the Donation was a fake.

questions.stem: Valla's treatise was most likely written to support

options.A: King Alfonso's quarrel with the pope over lands in Italy
options.B: Venice's efforts to protect its Mediterranean trade routes
options.C: the papacy's efforts to reunite the Greek and Latin churches
options.D: Italian rulers' plans for a crusade against the Ottomans

rationales.A: Correct. Valla worked for Alfonso, who was in conflict with Pope Eugenius IV over lands in southern Italy. Valla writes that it is "fairer to let the princes despoil you of all the empire you hold."
rationales.B: Incorrect. Valla attacks the pope's claims to land and power. He says nothing about Venetian trade.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Popes did work to reunite the Greek and Latin churches at this time, but Valla attacks the pope's claim to rule lands in the West.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Valla challenges the pope's claims to land. He does not call for war against the Ottomans.

questions.explanation: Valla served a king who was in conflict with the pope. By proving the Donation false, he attacked the pope's right to rule lands in Italy and the West.

questions.stem: Valla wrote in 1440, but his treatise became widely known only in the 1500s. Which of the following most directly made its wider readership possible?

options.A: The fall of Constantinople
options.B: The Concordat of Bologna
options.C: The printing press
options.D: The founding of the Jesuits

rationales.A: Incorrect. The fall of Constantinople in 1453 brought Greek scholars and manuscripts to Italy, but it did not spread Valla's Latin treatise.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The Concordat of Bologna (1516) gave the French king the right to name bishops. It had nothing to do with spreading Valla's work.
rationales.C: Correct. The German humanist Ulrich von Hutten printed the treatise in 1517, and printed copies spread quickly. Critics of the papacy, including Protestants, used it.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The Jesuits, founded in 1540, defended the pope's authority and did not spread attacks on it.

questions.explanation: Before printing, a work like Valla's survived in only a few handwritten copies. After Hutten printed it in 1517, readers across Europe could get it.

questions.stem: Henry VII's actions described in the passage best illustrate which of the following?

options.A: The spread of Protestant reform from the top down
options.B: The growth of Parliament's control over taxes and royal spending
options.C: The decline of royal courts in favor of church courts
options.D: The new monarchs' efforts to limit the power of the nobles

rationales.A: Incorrect. Protestant reform from the top down began under Henry VII's son, Henry VIII, in the 1530s.
rationales.B: Incorrect. English Parliaments had approved taxes since the Middle Ages, long before Henry VII. This passage is about the king using courts and fines to control nobles, not about Parliament gaining control over royal money.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The passage shows a royal court, the Star Chamber, gaining more authority.
rationales.D: Correct. Henry VII strengthened the Star Chamber, and Bacon reports that he fined the Earl of Oxford for keeping retainers. Like other new monarchs, he wanted to stop nobles from keeping private armies.

questions.explanation: After the Wars of the Roses, Henry VII wanted to end the private armies of great nobles. He passed laws against retainers and used royal courts and heavy fines to enforce them.

questions.stem: Which of the following is most important for a historian to consider when using the second paragraph as evidence about Henry VII?

options.A: Bacon wrote over a century later and calls the story a "report."
options.B: Bacon served in the Earl of Oxford's household and wanted to defend the earl.
options.C: Bacon was a Catholic who opposed the Tudor monarchy.
options.D: Bacon wrote the history to persuade Parliament to abolish the Star Chamber.

rationales.A: Correct. Henry VII died in 1509, and Bacon wrote in 1622. The story may be true, but Bacon himself calls it a "report" passed down over time.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Bacon did not serve in the earl's household, and the story makes the earl look guilty, not innocent.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Bacon was a Protestant who served Queen Elizabeth I and King James I.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Bacon describes the Star Chamber's powers without criticism. Parliament abolished it in 1641, long after Bacon's death in 1626.

questions.explanation: Bacon was a skilled writer and statesman, but he was not a witness. A story told for more than a hundred years may have changed, so historians check it against records from Henry VII's own time.

questions.stem: Henry VII's efforts to control the nobles were most similar to which of the following?

options.A: The Hanseatic League's trading privileges in the Baltic
options.B: The Golden Bull's confirmation of the German electors' privileges
options.C: The Italian city-states' hiring of mercenary captains
options.D: Ferdinand and Isabella's use of the Santa Hermandad

rationales.A: Incorrect. The Hanseatic League was a group of trading cities. It was not a ruler's effort to control nobles.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The Golden Bull of 1356 set rules for electing the emperor and confirmed the rights of the seven princes, called electors, who chose him. It made those princes stronger, not the emperor.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Hiring condottieri was a way for Italian states to fight wars, not a way to control the private armies of nobles.
rationales.D: Correct. Ferdinand and Isabella used a royal police force, the Santa Hermandad, to stop violence by nobles and to spread royal justice across Castile.

questions.explanation: The new monarchs of England, Spain, and France all worked to end private wars by nobles. They built royal courts, police forces, and armies loyal to the crown.

questions.stem: The Requirement is best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.A: Portuguese voyages to India around the southern tip of Africa
options.B: Spanish conquest of the Caribbean and Central America
options.C: The Protestant Reformation's attack on papal authority
options.D: Dutch competition for trade in the East Indies

rationales.A: Incorrect. Portuguese ships reached India in 1498, but the Requirement speaks of "these islands" and "Terra-firma" given to the Spanish monarchs.
rationales.B: Correct. By 1513 the Spanish had settled Hispaniola and Cuba and were moving onto the mainland of Central America. Commanders were told to read the Requirement before attacking Native peoples.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The Reformation began in 1517, after the Requirement was written, and the document supports the pope's authority.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The Dutch began trading in the East Indies around 1600, nearly a century later.

questions.explanation: The Requirement was written as Spain moved from the Caribbean islands to the American mainland. It shows how the Spanish crown tried to justify conquest.

questions.stem: The Requirement's statements about St. Peter and the pope's "donation" were most likely intended to

options.A: persuade the pope to grant Spain the right to explore
options.B: win Native allies for a war against Portugal
options.C: warn Spanish soldiers not to harm the Native peoples they met
options.D: give a religious and legal reason for Spanish conquest

rationales.A: Incorrect. The document says a pope had already "made donation of these isles and Terra-firma" to the Spanish monarchs.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The document does not mention Portugal. It demands that Native peoples accept Spanish rule.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The document threatens Native peoples with war and slavery if they do not obey.
rationales.D: Correct. By claiming that the pope, as St. Peter's successor, gave these lands to the Spanish monarchs, the document made war on those who refused to submit seem lawful.

questions.explanation: Christianity was both a reason for conquest and an excuse for it. The Requirement claimed that God, St. Peter, and the pope had given the land to Spain's rulers. So the deaths caused by resisting would be the Native peoples' own "fault."

questions.stem: Members of which of the following groups would have most strongly disagreed with the Requirement?

options.A: Spanish conquistadors such as Hernán Cortés and Francisco Pizarro
options.B: Dominican friars such as Bartolomé de Las Casas
options.C: Spanish settlers who held encomiendas
options.D: Lawyers who advised the Spanish crown

rationales.A: Incorrect. Conquistadors used documents like the Requirement to justify their attacks.
rationales.B: Correct. Las Casas and other Dominican friars protested the cruel treatment of Native peoples, and Las Casas mocked the Requirement as unjust and absurd.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Settlers who held encomiendas, grants of Native labor, gained from the conquest and supported it.
rationales.D: Incorrect. A royal legal adviser, Palacios Rubios, wrote the Requirement for the crown.

questions.explanation: Some Spanish friars said Native peoples were being treated unjustly. Two famous Dominicans were Antonio de Montesinos and Bartolomé de Las Casas. Their protests led to debates in Spain about the conquest.

questions.stem: Source 1 is best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.A: The growth of English sugar plantations in Barbados
options.B: The Dutch capture of Portugal's trading posts in Africa
options.C: The collapse of the Native population of the Caribbean islands
options.D: The spread of serfdom in eastern Europe

rationales.A: Incorrect. The English settled Barbados in 1627, more than a century after this license.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The Dutch took some Portuguese posts in Africa in the 1600s, long after 1518.
rationales.C: Correct. By 1518, disease, war, and forced labor had killed most of the Taíno people of Hispaniola and the other islands. Spanish colonists wanted new sources of labor.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Serfdom was growing in eastern Europe, but it had nothing to do with sending enslaved Africans to the Americas.

questions.explanation: The license lets Gorrevod ship 4,000 enslaved Africans to Spain's colonies. The king allowed this because Native people in the Caribbean were dying fast. Colonists wanted new workers.

questions.stem: Source 1's statement that enslaved people were usually brought from "the isles of Guinea" to "these realms and to Portugal" best reflects which of the following?

options.A: Spain's control of the West African coast under the Treaty of Tordesillas
options.B: the Portuguese trading network along the coast of West Africa
options.C: Dutch leadership of the Atlantic slave trade in the early 1500s
options.D: the Ottoman Empire's control of trade routes across the Sahara

rationales.A: Incorrect. The Treaty of Tordesillas placed Africa on Portugal's side of the line, so Spain had to rely on Portuguese and other traders.
rationales.B: Correct. In the 1400s and 1500s the Portuguese set up trading posts along the African coast. They bought enslaved Africans there and shipped them to Portugal, Spain, and later the Americas.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The Dutch did not enter the Atlantic slave trade on a large scale until the 1600s.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The license describes shipping by sea from the West African coast, where the Portuguese, not the Ottomans, ran the trade.

questions.explanation: Portuguese sailors explored the African coast in the 1400s. They built forts such as Elmina in 1482. By 1518 Portuguese traders sold enslaved Africans in Portugal and Spain, and Spain's license depended on them.

questions.stem: In Source 2, Brandão argues that the slave trade is acceptable mainly because

options.A: the Africans who are sold have been fairly convicted of crimes
options.B: the Spanish king has promised to free the enslaved after they become Christians
options.C: church authorities approved it, and many of the enslaved will be saved
options.D: Portuguese law requires traders to prove that each captive was taken legally

rationales.A: Incorrect. Brandão admits that some were "stolen" or sold "for offenses so slight that they do not deserve captivity."
rationales.B: Incorrect. Brandão says nothing about freeing the enslaved. He says the Jesuits "buy these slaves for our service."
rationales.C: Correct. Brandão points to the "Board of Conscience in Lisbon," the bishops, and "very learned Fathers." He adds that "those who find salvation are many."
rationales.D: Incorrect. Brandão says that checking how each captive was taken "is an impossibility."

questions.explanation: Brandão gives religious reasons for the trade. Church leaders approved it, he says, and many of the enslaved will be "saved." Religion was used both to drive European expansion and to excuse it.

questions.stem: Taken together, the two sources best illustrate which change between 1518 and 1610?

options.A: Church leaders turned against the slave trade and persuaded rulers to limit it.
options.B: England and the Dutch Republic replaced Portugal as the main suppliers of enslaved Africans.
options.C: The shipment of enslaved Africans to the Americas grew into a large, regular trade.
options.D: Enslaved Africans were increasingly sent to Europe rather than to the Americas.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Brandão reports that learned churchmen approved the trade: "never did they consider this trade as illicit." The trade kept growing.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The Dutch and English became major slave traders only later in the 1600s. In 1610 the Portuguese still led the trade.
rationales.C: Correct. In 1518 enslaved Africans were usually brought "to these realms and to Portugal," and shipping 4,000 people straight to the Indies needed the king's special permission. In 1610 Brandão says that "ten or twelve thousand" leave the single port of Luanda "every year."
rationales.D: Incorrect. Brandão writes to a priest in the Spanish colonies about Africans "who are sent to your parts," that is, to the Americas.

questions.explanation: In 1518, the license says, enslaved Africans were usually brought to Spain and Portugal, and the king had to give special permission to ship them straight to the Americas. Between 1518 and 1610, sugar plantations spread in Brazil and the Caribbean, and the demand for enslaved workers grew. The Atlantic slave trade became a huge, organized business.
